text: Wouldn't it be the most ridiculous story ever told if the boy who couldn't read and write at 18 gets a PhD before he's 30? That's Cambridge professor Jason Ardé and his story is the most ridiculous ever told but he didn't do it alone. And sometimes you don't need a thousand people to want you to win. You just need one or two. Jason's story got off to a tough start. He was diagnosed with autism and global development delay and was nonverbal. My processing is very, very slow. So cognitively that has always been a problem. That's the reason why things happen later for me than they should have done four or five hours of speech therapy a day from the age of three. There is nothing to suggest that any of this is working at 11. Going to this room we go through the same kind of warm exercise as we normally did. The speech therapist said to me, hello Jason, she always did. And I just responded hello. It's quite a strange thing to hear your own voice for the first time when you're 11. I didn't expect my voice to sound like this. I think the first time I saw I was like 15. That was like an experience. I was all gazmic. Oh I need swear words. Like am I using them in the right context? Jason's mother was the first to instill in him a valuable life lesson. So she had done a lot of research herself. She knew that an autistic trait was repetition. She normalised things a lot. In a sport like snooker, repetition is quite an important thing. You assess the shot, you cue the shot, you feather. It's the same thing over and over and over again. And her whole thing was that he might be able to apply it to other areas of his life. For example, speaking and in particular being illiterate. It's hard to say if it worked or not. Well in terms of snooker it did because I became a really good snooker player. But having a strategy to succeed in life wasn't enough. Jason still needed something we could all do with. A good teacher. I think teachers who care are absolutely vital. The caring side of education is the most important thing. When I was with him in his classes he just didn't make me feel any different. And he just took an interest. He took such an interest. He gave people the most important thing you can give any human being. He gave them agency. And the sense of importance and just always felt like he wanted me to win. Hearing that Jason looked up to me and valued me is actually really humbling. And it just makes you very aware that as a teacher the impact you can have is huge. If I hadn't met Sandra I wouldn't be sat in front of you now. Jason has been a special case I think in my life. I met him in 2003. He didn't know how to write. I felt something on the day. I must help this guy. There was something about Sandra's approach that took Jason back to his past. And this time he was ready. Sandra's whole thing was repetition. Just doing phonics, doing literacy, doing reading and writing over and over again. I went over and over and over with the same topics until he is mastering it. Tell me every day you're great. You're going to do something great every single day. But you have to be disciplined Jason. You need someone to say look you're capable of doing things. You can achieve it. You know let's do it together. One of the things he said to me is like look Jason you have this indomitable will. That is going to be your thing. Then I kind of thought right I'm just going to try as hard as possible. So when I got to university that's the approach I took. Now Jason being Jason he didn't just stop at university. In my second year of uni I had a lecturer who just got their PhD. Kind of went back and said to Sandra like what's a PhD? I want to try and do one. And he said Jason we can do this. And once Jason started he couldn't stop. He made it all the way to becoming one of the youngest professors ever at Cambridge. And it might not stop there. All of these lessons go back to being 14, 15, 16 being taught these things by Mr. Trace. And then it kind of being taken to another level with Sandra and working on the fact that my only two strengths are that I've got a lot of will. I'm tonation. I'm good with people. And I remember standing there thinking you're in a situation where you're in the cusp of doing something that you've always wanted to do. Enjoy it.
